claim: Exophilin-8-knockout mice showed slightly reduced body weight compared to wild-type mice.
source: However, they showed slightly reduced body weight and significantly higher blood glucose levels after a glucose load, although their insulin sensitivity was not altered (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from measurements in age-matched wild-type and knockout mice showing body weight differences.

claim: Exophilin-8-knockout mice showed significantly higher blood glucose levels after a glucose load compared to wild-type mice.
source: However, they showed slightly reduced body weight and significantly higher blood glucose levels after a glucose load, although their insulin sensitivity was not altered (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests showing elevated blood glucose in knockout mice.

claim: Exophilin-8-knockout mice showed no alteration in insulin sensitivity compared to wild-type mice.
source: However, they showed slightly reduced body weight and significantly higher blood glucose levels after a glucose load, although their insulin sensitivity was not altered (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from intraperitoneal insulin tolerance tests showing no significant difference between wild-type and knockout mice.

claim: Exophilin-8 was expressed in pancreatic islets, pituitary, and brain.
source: Exophilin-8 was expressed in pancreatic islets, as well as in pituitary and brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblotting data showing exophilin-8 protein expression in these tissues.

claim: Absence of exophilin-8 induced decreased insulin secretion in response to glucose in isolated islets.
source: Further, its absence induced decreased insulin secretion in responses to glucose, potassium, or forskolin (an activator of adenylate cyclase) with glucose (Figure 1B–D), but did not change secretion in response to phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA; a protein kinase C activator) with glucose (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents perifusion data showing reduced insulin secretion in knockout islets stimulated with glucose.

claim: Absence of exophilin-8 induced decreased insulin secretion in response to potassium in isolated islets.
source: Further, its absence induced decreased insulin secretion in responses to glucose, potassium, or forskolin (an activator of adenylate cyclase) with glucose (Figure 1B–D), but did not change secretion in response to phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA; a protein kinase C activator) with glucose (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents perifusion data showing reduced insulin secretion in knockout islets stimulated with potassium.

claim: Absence of exophilin-8 induced decreased insulin secretion in response to forskolin with glucose in isolated islets.
source: Further, its absence induced decreased insulin secretion in responses to glucose, potassium, or forskolin (an activator of adenylate cyclase) with glucose (Figure 1B–D), but did not change secretion in response to phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA; a protein kinase C activator) with glucose (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents perifusion data showing reduced insulin secretion in knockout islets stimulated with forskolin and glucose.

claim: Absence of exophilin-8 did not change insulin secretion in response to PMA with glucose in isolated islets.
source: Further, its absence induced decreased insulin secretion in responses to glucose, potassium, or forskolin (an activator of adenylate cyclase) with glucose (Figure 1B–D), but did not change secretion in response to phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA; a protein kinase C activator) with glucose (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents perifusion data showing no significant difference in insulin secretion between wild-type and knockout islets stimulated with PMA and glucose.

claim: Forskolin is an activator of adenylate cyclase.
source: Further, its absence induced decreased insulin secretion in responses to glucose, potassium, or forskolin (an activator of adenylate cyclase) with glucose (Figure 1B–D), but did not change secretion in response to phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA; a protein kinase C activator) with glucose (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: PMA is a protein kinase C activator.
source: Further, its absence induced decreased insulin secretion in responses to glucose, potassium, or forskolin (an activator of adenylate cyclase) with glucose (Figure 1B–D), but did not change secretion in response to phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA; a protein kinase C activator) with glucose (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical F-actin-disrupting PMA might negate the function of exophilin-8 that is localized within the actin cortex.
source: Cortical F-actin-disrupting PMA (Vitale et al., 1995) might negate the function of exophilin-8 that is localized within the actin cortex (Desnos et al., 2003; Waselle et al., 2003; Mizuno et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on previous literature and the current experimental results.

claim: PMA disrupts cortical F-actin.
source: Cortical F-actin-disrupting PMA (Vitale et al., 1995) might negate the function of exophilin-8 that is localized within the actin cortex (Desnos et al., 2003; Waselle et al., 2003; Mizuno et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vitale et al., 1995.

claim: Exophilin-8 is localized within the actin cortex.
source: Cortical F-actin-disrupting PMA (Vitale et al., 1995) might negate the function of exophilin-8 that is localized within the actin cortex (Desnos et al., 2003; Waselle et al., 2003; Mizuno et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desnos et al., 2003; Waselle et al., 2003; Mizuno et al., 2011.

claim: Insulin granules were preferentially polarized close to the cell edges in wild-type islets.
source: Although the antibodies were accessible to only surface β-cells, insulin granules were preferentially polarized close to the cell edges in wild-type islets, whereas they were diffusely distributed in the perinuclear cytoplasm in exophilin-8-null islets (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing polarized insulin granule distribution in wild-type islets.

claim: Insulin granules were diffusely distributed in the perinuclear cytoplasm in exophilin-8-null islets.
source: Although the antibodies were accessible to only surface β-cells, insulin granules were preferentially polarized close to the cell edges in wild-type islets, whereas they were diffusely distributed in the perinuclear cytoplasm in exophilin-8-null islets (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing diffuse insulin granule distribution in knockout islets.

claim: Exophilin-8-null β-cells have a significantly lower number of granules that have centers within 300 nm of the plasma membrane.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that exophilin-8-null β-cells have a significantly lower number of granules that have centers within 300 nm of the plasma membrane (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data showing reduced granule numbers near the plasma membrane in knockout cells.

claim: Exophilin-8-null β-cells still exhibited granules directly attached to the plasma membrane.
source: Notably, however, they still exhibited granules directly attached to the plasma membrane (see arrows in Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy images showing docked granules in knockout cells.

claim: RIM-BP2 was identified as a binding partner of exophilin-8 by LC-MS/MS analysis.
source: Among the protein bands specific for the MEF-exophilin-8 eluate (Figure 3A), those with the highest molecular mass (150 ~ 190 kDa) were identified as RIM-BP2 and myosin-VIIa by a liquid chromatography (LC)-tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) analysis.
evidence: The manuscript presents LC-MS/MS data identifying RIM-BP2 in the exophilin-8 immunoprecipitate.

claim: Myosin-VIIa was identified as a binding partner of exophilin-8 by LC-MS/MS analysis.
source: Among the protein bands specific for the MEF-exophilin-8 eluate (Figure 3A), those with the highest molecular mass (150 ~ 190 kDa) were identified as RIM-BP2 and myosin-VIIa by a liquid chromatography (LC)-tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) analysis.
evidence: The manuscript presents LC-MS/MS data identifying myosin-VIIa in the exophilin-8 immunoprecipitate.

claim: The interaction between exophilin-8 and myosin-VIIa was already known.
source: Because the interaction with myosin-VIIa was already known, we further investigated that with RIM-BP2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of RIM-BP2 in the immunoprecipitate of MEF-exophilin-8 in MIN6 cells was confirmed.
source: We confirmed the presence of RIM-BP2 in the immunoprecipitate of MEF-exophilin-8 in MIN6 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data confirming the interaction between exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2 in MIN6 cells.

claim: The endogenous complex between exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2 was identified in INS-1 823/13 cells.
source: We also identified the endogenous complex between the two proteins in another β-cell line, INS-1 823/13 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing endogenous interaction between exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2 in INS-1 823/13 cells.

claim: RIM-BP2 was downregulated in exophilin-8-null pancreatic islets.
source: Although RIM-BP2 was downregulated in exophilin-8-null pancreatic islets (Figure 3D), it was expressed in wild-type islets and in these β-cell lines at even higher levels than in brain (Figure 3E), where it was initially identified (Wang et al., 2000; Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblotting data showing reduced RIM-BP2 protein levels in knockout islets.

claim: RIM-BP2 was expressed in wild-type islets at even higher levels than in brain.
source: Although RIM-BP2 was downregulated in exophilin-8-null pancreatic islets (Figure 3D), it was expressed in wild-type islets and in these β-cell lines at even higher levels than in brain (Figure 3E), where it was initially identified (Wang et al., 2000; Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblotting data comparing RIM-BP2 expression levels across tissues.

claim: RIM-BP2 was initially identified in brain.
source: Although RIM-BP2 was downregulated in exophilin-8-null pancreatic islets (Figure 3D), it was expressed in wild-type islets and in these β-cell lines at even higher levels than in brain (Figure 3E), where it was initially identified (Wang et al., 2000; Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000; Hibino et al., 2002.

claim: RIM-BP2 has three separate SH3 domains and three contiguous fibronectin type III (FNIII) domains.
source: RIM-BP2 has three separate SH3 domains and three contiguous fibronectin type III (FNIII) domains (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the protein structure.

claim: The first SH3 domain of RIM-BP2 significantly interacted with exophilin-8 when expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: When expressed in HEK293A cells, the first SH3 domain significantly, and the third SH3 domain strongly, interacted with exophilin-8, although the second SH3 domain or the whole FNIII domains did not (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between the first SH3 domain and exophilin-8.

claim: The third SH3 domain of RIM-BP2 strongly interacted with exophilin-8 when expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: When expressed in HEK293A cells, the first SH3 domain significantly, and the third SH3 domain strongly, interacted with exophilin-8, although the second SH3 domain or the whole FNIII domains did not (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing strong interaction between the third SH3 domain and exophilin-8.

claim: The second SH3 domain of RIM-BP2 did not interact with exophilin-8 when expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: When expressed in HEK293A cells, the first SH3 domain significantly, and the third SH3 domain strongly, interacted with exophilin-8, although the second SH3 domain or the whole FNIII domains did not (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing no interaction between the second SH3 domain and exophilin-8.

claim: The whole FNIII domains of RIM-BP2 did not interact with exophilin-8 when expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: When expressed in HEK293A cells, the first SH3 domain significantly, and the third SH3 domain strongly, interacted with exophilin-8, although the second SH3 domain or the whole FNIII domains did not (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing no interaction between the FNIII domains and exophilin-8.

claim: Exophilin-8 can be divided into Rab27-binding domain (RBD), myosin-binding domain (MBD), and actin-binding domain (ABD).
source: Exophilin-8 can be divided into Rab27-binding domain (RBD), myosin-binding domain (MBD), and actin-binding domain (ABD) (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002.

claim: The C-terminus of exophilin-8 containing ABD bound RIM-BP2.
source: The C-terminus of exophilin-8 containing ABD bound RIM-BP2, although the N-terminus consisting of RBD and MBD did not (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing binding between the C-terminus of exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2.

claim: The N-terminus of exophilin-8 consisting of RBD and MBD did not bind RIM-BP2.
source: The C-terminus of exophilin-8 containing ABD bound RIM-BP2, although the N-terminus consisting of RBD and MBD did not (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing no binding between the N-terminus of exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2.

claim: Exophilin-8 has two SH3 domain-interacting proline-rich sequences, RXXPXXP.
source: Exophilin-8 has two SH3 domain-interacting proline-rich sequences, RXXPXXP (Mayer, 2001), at residues 474–480 in the MBD and at residues 798–804 in the ABD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis and citation to Mayer, 2001.

claim: RXXPXXP is an SH3 domain-interacting proline-rich sequence.
source: Exophilin-8 has two SH3 domain-interacting proline-rich sequences, RXXPXXP (Mayer, 2001), at residues 474–480 in the MBD and at residues 798–804 in the ABD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mayer, 2001.

claim: The PA mutant replacing arginine and proline residues with alanine residues in the motif of ABD disrupted the interaction with RIM-BP2.
source: Consistent with the finding of the above binding experiments (Figure 4C), the PA mutant replacing arginine and proline residues with alanine residues in the motif of ABD, but not that of MBD, disrupted the interaction with RIM-BP2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing loss of interaction between the PA (ABD) mutant and RIM-BP2.

claim: The PA mutant replacing arginine and proline residues with alanine residues in the motif of MBD did not disrupt the interaction with RIM-BP2.
source: Consistent with the finding of the above binding experiments (Figure 4C), the PA mutant replacing arginine and proline residues with alanine residues in the motif of ABD, but not that of MBD, disrupted the interaction with RIM-BP2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing preserved interaction between the PA (MBD) mutant and RIM-BP2.

claim: Wild-type exophilin-8, but not the PA (ABD) mutant, interacts with endogenous RIM-BP2 in MIN6 cells.
source: We further confirmed that wild-type exophilin-8, but not the PA (ABD) mutant, interacts with endogenous RIM-BP2 in MIN6 cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between wild-type exophilin-8 and endogenous RIM-BP2, but not with the PA (ABD) mutant.

claim: The two proteins interact between the first and/or third SH domains in RIM-BP2 and the C-terminal RXXPXXP sequence in exophilin-8.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that the two proteins interact between the first and/or third SH domains in RIM-BP2 and the C-terminal RXXPXXP sequence in exophilin-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding domain mapping experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Exogenously expressed exophilin-8 redistributes secretory granules to the cell corners and/or the tips of cell extensions.
source: Exogenously expressed exophilin-8 redistributes secretory granules to the cell corners and/or the tips of cell extensions (Mizuno et al., 2011; Huet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mizuno et al., 2011; Huet et al., 2012.

claim: Both RIM-BP2 and exophilin-8 are endogenously colocalized with insulin granules, especially those accumulated at the cell corners, in INS-1 832/13 cells.
source: Immunostaining experiments have revealed that both RIM-BP2 and exophilin-8 are endogenously colocalized with insulin granules, especially those accumulated at the cell corners, in INS-1 832/13 cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing colocalization of RIM-BP2 and exophilin-8 with insulin granules.

claim: Wild-type exophilin-8 is colocalized with RIM-BP2 and accumulates both insulin granules and RIM-BP2 at the cell corners.
source: We found that wild-type exophilin-8 is colocalized with RIM-BP2 and accumulates both insulin granules and RIM-BP2 at the cell corners (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing colocalization and accumulation of exophilin-8, RIM-BP2, and insulin granules at cell corners.

claim: The PA (ABD) mutant deficient in binding activity to RIM-BP2 was not polarized at the cell corners and dispersed insulin granules and RIM-BP2 diffusively in the cytoplasm.
source: By contrast, the PA (ABD) mutant deficient in binding activity to RIM-BP2 was not polarized at the cell corners and dispersed insulin granules and RIM-BP2 diffusively in the cytoplasm.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing diffuse distribution of the PA (ABD) mutant, insulin granules, and RIM-BP2.

claim: Exophilin-8 induces peripheral localization of insulin granules through the interaction with RIM-BP2.
source: These findings indicate that exophilin-8 induces peripheral localization of insulin granules through the interaction with RIM-BP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining experiments showing that the PA (ABD) mutant, which cannot bind RIM-BP2, fails to accumulate granules peripherally.

claim: Wild-type exophilin-8 expressed at the endogenous protein level increased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in exophilin-8-null islets.
source: Although wild-type exophilin-8 expressed at the endogenous protein level increased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, the PA (ABD) mutant failed to do so (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing rescue of secretion by wild-type exophilin-8 in knockout islets.

claim: The PA (ABD) mutant failed to increase glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in exophilin-8-null islets.
source: Although wild-type exophilin-8 expressed at the endogenous protein level increased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, the PA (ABD) mutant failed to do so (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing no rescue of secretion by the PA (ABD) mutant in knockout islets.

claim: Overexpression of RIM-BP2 significantly enhanced insulin secretion in wild-type islets.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of RIM-BP2 significantly enhanced insulin secretion in wild-type islets, but not in exophilin-8-null islets (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing enhanced secretion with RIM-BP2 overexpression in wild-type islets.

claim: Overexpression of RIM-BP2 did not enhance insulin secretion in exophilin-8-null islets.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of RIM-BP2 significantly enhanced insulin secretion in wild-type islets, but not in exophilin-8-null islets (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing no enhancement of secretion with RIM-BP2 overexpression in knockout islets.

claim: A similar secretion-promoting effect of RIM-BP2 was observed in MIN6 cells, but not in the exophilin-8-null β-cell line.
source: A similar secretion-promoting effect of RIM-BP2 was observed in MIN6 cells, but not in the exophilin-8-null β-cell line (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), which was generated by a method similar to that by which the 'wild-type' MIN6 cell line was previously established (Miyazaki et al., 1990).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing enhanced secretion with RIM-BP2 overexpression in MIN6 cells but not in exophilin-8-null β-cell line.

claim: RIM-BP2ΔSH3 loses the binding activity to exophilin-8.
source: We then generated RIM-BP2 lacking all the three SH3 domains (RIM-BP2ΔSH3), and confirmed that this mutant loses the binding activity to exophilin-8 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing no binding between RIM-BP2ΔSH3 and exophilin-8.

claim: When overexpressed in MIN6 cells, only wild-type RIM-BP2, but not RIM-BP2ΔSH3, enhanced insulin secretion.
source: When overexpressed in MIN6 cells, only wild-type RIM-BP2, but not RIM-BP2ΔSH3, enhanced insulin secretion (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing enhanced secretion with wild-type RIM-BP2 but not with RIM-BP2ΔSH3.

claim: The secretion-promoting activity of exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 requires the interaction with the other protein.
source: These findings indicate that the secretion-promoting activity of exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 requires the interaction with the other protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that mutants unable to interact fail to promote secretion.

claim: Exogenous or endogenous RIM-BP2 expressed in β-cells exhibited a doublet in gels.
source: Although exogenous or endogenous RIM-BP2 expressed in β-cells exhibited a doublet in gels (Figure 3E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D), both bands were specifically downregulated by small interfering RNA (siRNA) against RIM-BP2 (Figure 7A), suggesting that they represent differentially modified RIM-BP2.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblotting data showing two bands for RIM-BP2.

claim: Both bands of RIM-BP2 were specifically downregulated by siRNA against RIM-BP2.
source: Although exogenous or endogenous RIM-BP2 expressed in β-cells exhibited a doublet in gels (Figure 3E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D), both bands were specifically downregulated by small interfering RNA (siRNA) against RIM-BP2 (Figure 7A), suggesting that they represent differentially modified RIM-BP2.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblotting data showing downregulation of both RIM-BP2 bands by siRNA.

claim: The two bands of RIM-BP2 represent differentially modified RIM-BP2.
source: Although exogenous or endogenous RIM-BP2 expressed in β-cells exhibited a doublet in gels (Figure 3E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D), both bands were specifically downregulated by small interfering RNA (siRNA) against RIM-BP2 (Figure 7A), suggesting that they represent differentially modified RIM-BP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both bands are downregulated by siRNA against RIM-BP2.

claim: Exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 knockdown profoundly decreased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: Exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 knockdown profoundly decreased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing decreased secretion with exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 knockdown.

claim: Either exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 knockdown induced diffusive redistributions of granules and the other protein in the cytoplasm.
source: Furthermore, either type of knockdown induced diffusive redistributions of granules and the other protein in the cytoplasm (Figure 7C–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing diffuse distribution of granules and proteins with knockdown.

claim: Both exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2 are necessary for peripheral accumulation and efficient exocytosis of secretory granules.
source: Therefore, both exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2 are necessary for peripheral accumulation and efficient exocytosis of secretory granules.
evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown experiments showing that loss of either protein disrupts granule localization and secretion.

claim: When wild-type or ΔSH3 RIM-BP2 was expressed in RIM-BP2-knockdown cells, only the wild type rescued the decreased insulin secretion and restored the peripheral granule accumulation.
source: When wild-type or ΔSH3 RIM-BP2 was expressed in RIM-BP2-knockdown cells, only the wild type rescued the decreased insulin secretion and restored the peripheral granule accumulation (Figure 7F,G, Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3), again supporting the importance of the complex formation between the two proteins.
evidence: The manuscript presents rescue experiment data showing that only wild-type RIM-BP2 restores secretion and granule localization.

claim: The rescue experiments support the importance of the complex formation between exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2.
source: When wild-type or ΔSH3 RIM-BP2 was expressed in RIM-BP2-knockdown cells, only the wild type rescued the decreased insulin secretion and restored the peripheral granule accumulation (Figure 7F,G, Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3), again supporting the importance of the complex formation between the two proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that the ΔSH3 mutant, which cannot bind exophilin-8, fails to rescue.

claim: Wild-type exophilin-8, but not the PA (ABD) mutant, coprecipitated RIM-BP2 in INS-1 832/13 cells expressing HA-tagged RIM-BP2.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, the wild type, but not the PA (ABD) mutant, coprecipitated RIM-BP2, and concordantly interacted with RIM-BP2-interacting Cav1.3 and RIM, and RIM-interacting Munc13-1, as has been observed in neurons (Wang et al., 2000; Betz et al., 2001; Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing coprecipitation of RIM-BP2 with wild-type exophilin-8 but not with the PA (ABD) mutant.

claim: Wild-type exophilin-8 interacted with RIM-BP2-interacting Cav1.3 and RIM, and RIM-interacting Munc13-1.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, the wild type, but not the PA (ABD) mutant, coprecipitated RIM-BP2, and concordantly interacted with RIM-BP2-interacting Cav1.3 and RIM, and RIM-interacting Munc13-1, as has been observed in neurons (Wang et al., 2000; Betz et al., 2001; Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing interaction of wild-type exophilin-8 with Cav1.3, RIM, and Munc13-1.

claim: RIM-BP2 interacts with Cav1.3 and RIM in neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, the wild type, but not the PA (ABD) mutant, coprecipitated RIM-BP2, and concordantly interacted with RIM-BP2-interacting Cav1.3 and RIM, and RIM-interacting Munc13-1, as has been observed in neurons (Wang et al., 2000; Betz et al., 2001; Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000; Betz et al., 2001; Hibino et al., 2002.

claim: RIM interacts with Munc13-1 in neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, the wild type, but not the PA (ABD) mutant, coprecipitated RIM-BP2, and concordantly interacted with RIM-BP2-interacting Cav1.3 and RIM, and RIM-interacting Munc13-1, as has been observed in neurons (Wang et al., 2000; Betz et al., 2001; Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000; Betz et al., 2001; Hibino et al., 2002.

claim: Both wild-type and PA (ABD) mutant exophilin-8 interacted with previously known exophilin-8-interacting proteins, such as Rab27a, protein kinase A (PKA), Sec6, and actin.
source: By contrast, both the wild type and the mutant interacted with previously known exophilin-8-interacting proteins, such as Rab27a, protein kinase A (PKA), Sec6 (Goehring et al., 2007), and actin.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing interaction of both wild-type and PA (ABD) mutant with Rab27a, PKA, Sec6, and actin.

claim: Myosin-Va was not found in the immunoprecipitate of either wild-type or mutant exophilin-8.
source: However, myosin-Va was not found in the immunoprecipitate of either wild-type or mutant exophilin-8, but was easily detected in that of exophilin-3 (also known as melanophilin and Slac2a; Figure 8B), another Rab27 effector that exhibits binding activity to myosin-Va (Fukuda et al., 2002; Nagashima et al., 2002; Strom et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing no interaction between exophilin-8 and myosin-Va.

claim: Myosin-Va was easily detected in the immunoprecipitate of exophilin-3.
source: However, myosin-Va was not found in the immunoprecipitate of either wild-type or mutant exophilin-8, but was easily detected in that of exophilin-3 (also known as melanophilin and Slac2a; Figure 8B), another Rab27 effector that exhibits binding activity to myosin-Va (Fukuda et al., 2002; Nagashima et al., 2002; Strom et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between exophilin-3 and myosin-Va.

claim: Exophilin-3 is another Rab27 effector that exhibits binding activity to myosin-Va.
source: However, myosin-Va was not found in the immunoprecipitate of either wild-type or mutant exophilin-8, but was easily detected in that of exophilin-3 (also known as melanophilin and Slac2a; Figure 8B), another Rab27 effector that exhibits binding activity to myosin-Va (Fukuda et al., 2002; Nagashima et al., 2002; Strom et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fukuda et al., 2002; Nagashima et al., 2002; Strom et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2002.

claim: Myosin-VIIa was identified in the immunoprecipitate of exophilin-8.
source: Instead, we identified myosin-VIIa in the immunoprecipitate, the tail domain of which has been reported to interact with exophilin-8 in both heterologous cells and in vitro (El-Amraoui et al., 2002; Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between exophilin-8 and myosin-VIIa.

claim: The tail domain of myosin-VIIa has been reported to interact with exophilin-8 in both heterologous cells and in vitro.
source: Instead, we identified myosin-VIIa in the immunoprecipitate, the tail domain of which has been reported to interact with exophilin-8 in both heterologous cells and in vitro (El-Amraoui et al., 2002; Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to El-Amraoui et al., 2002; Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002.

claim: The PA (ABD) exophilin-8 failed to interact with myosin-VIIa.
source: Unexpectedly, however, the PA (ABD) exophilin-8, despite the mutation outside of MBD, failed to interact with myosin-VIIa.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing no interaction between the PA (ABD) mutant and myosin-VIIa.

claim: The same proline motif of exophilin-8 is involved in binding with myosin-VIIa as well as with RIM-BP2, or exophilin-8 indirectly interacts with myosin-VIIa through RIM-BP2.
source: This finding indicates that the same proline motif of exophilin-8 is involved in binding with myosin-VIIa as well as with RIM-BP2, or that exophilin-8 indirectly interacts with myosin-VIIa through RIM-BP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the PA (ABD) mutant fails to bind both RIM-BP2 and myosin-VIIa.

claim: The interaction between RIM-BP2 and myosin-VIIa persists in the exophilin-8-null β-cell line.
source: We found that the interaction persists in the exophilin-8-null β-cell line and is preserved by the exogenous expression of wild-type exophilin-8 (Figure 8C), indicating that RIM-BP2, but not exophilin-8, is primarily involved in the interaction with myosin-VIIa in cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between RIM-BP2 and myosin-VIIa in exophilin-8-null cells.

claim: RIM-BP2, but not exophilin-8, is primarily involved in the interaction with myosin-VIIa in cells.
source: We found that the interaction persists in the exophilin-8-null β-cell line and is preserved by the exogenous expression of wild-type exophilin-8 (Figure 8C), indicating that RIM-BP2, but not exophilin-8, is primarily involved in the interaction with myosin-VIIa in cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RIM-BP2 and myosin-VIIa interact in the absence of exophilin-8.

claim: Wild-type, but not PA mutant, exophilin-8 ABD bound RIM-BP2 when simultaneously expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: As expected, wild-type, but not PA mutant, exophilin-8 ABD bound RIM-BP2, strongly indicating the direct interaction because there were no other specific proteins (Figure 9A, lanes 2 and 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents pull-down data showing binding between wild-type exophilin-8 ABD and RIM-BP2 but not with the PA mutant.

claim: The binding between wild-type exophilin-8 ABD and RIM-BP2 strongly indicates direct interaction because there were no other specific proteins.
source: As expected, wild-type, but not PA mutant, exophilin-8 ABD bound RIM-BP2, strongly indicating the direct interaction because there were no other specific proteins (Figure 9A, lanes 2 and 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the pull-down experiment showing only the two proteins in the complex.

claim: Both wild-type and PA mutant exophilin-8 ABD bound myosin-VIIa with or without RIM-BP2 expression in HEK293A cells.
source: Unexpectedly, however, both wild-type and PA mutant exophilin-8 ABD bound myosin-VIIa with or without RIM-BP2 expression (Figure 9A, lanes 3, 4, 6, and 7), in contrast to the finding in INS-1 832/13 cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript presents pull-down data showing binding between both wild-type and PA mutant exophilin-8 ABD and myosin-VIIa.

claim: Exophilin-8 seems to directly interact with myosin-VIIa at least in heterologous cells.
source: Therefore, exophilin-8 seems to directly interact with myosin-VIIa at least in heterologous cells, consistent with the previous findings (El-Amraoui et al., 2002; Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002), and furthermore, this interaction does not require the MBD or the proline-rich motif in the ABD of exophilin-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the pull-down experiments in HEK293A cells and supported by previous literature.

claim: The interaction between exophilin-8 and myosin-VIIa does not require the MBD or the proline-rich motif in the ABD of exophilin-8.
source: Therefore, exophilin-8 seems to directly interact with myosin-VIIa at least in heterologous cells, consistent with the previous findings (El-Amraoui et al., 2002; Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002), and furthermore, this interaction does not require the MBD or the proline-rich motif in the ABD of exophilin-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the PA mutant, which lacks the proline-rich motif, still binds myosin-VIIa in HEK293A cells.

claim: RIM-BP2 bound wild-type, but not PA mutant, exophilin-8 ABD when expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: We confirmed that RIM-BP2 bound wild-type, but not PA mutant, exophilin-8 ABD (Figure 9B, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents pull-down data showing binding between RIM-BP2 and wild-type exophilin-8 ABD but not with the PA mutant.

claim: RIM-BP2 could not bind myosin-VIIa without simultaneous expression of wild-type exophilin8 ABD.
source: However, RIM-BP2 could not bind myosin-VIIa without simultaneous expression of wild-type exophilin8 ABD (Figure 9B, lanes 4–6), indicating that RIM-BP2 cannot directly bind myosin-VIIa.
evidence: The manuscript presents pull-down data showing no binding between RIM-BP2 and myosin-VIIa in the absence of wild-type exophilin-8 ABD.

claim: RIM-BP2 cannot directly bind myosin-VIIa.
source: However, RIM-BP2 could not bind myosin-VIIa without simultaneous expression of wild-type exophilin8 ABD (Figure 9B, lanes 4–6), indicating that RIM-BP2 cannot directly bind myosin-VIIa.
evidence: This is inferred from the pull-down experiment showing that RIM-BP2 requires exophilin-8 to bind myosin-VIIa.

claim: The approximate molecular mass by SDS-PAGE of myosin-VIIa expressed in HEK293A cells is ~260 kDa corresponding to its calculated molecular mass.
source: We noticed that, although the approximate molecular mass by sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) of myosin-VIIa expressed in HEK293A cells is ~260 kDa corresponding to its calculated molecular mass (Figure 9A,B), that of myosin VIIa interacting with RIM-BP2 in β-cell lines is ~170 kDa (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: The manuscript presents gel electrophoresis data showing myosin-VIIa at ~260 kDa in HEK293A cells.

claim: The molecular mass of myosin-VIIa interacting with RIM-BP2 in β-cell lines is ~170 kDa.
source: We noticed that, although the approximate molecular mass by sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) of myosin-VIIa expressed in HEK293A cells is ~260 kDa corresponding to its calculated molecular mass (Figure 9A,B), that of myosin VIIa interacting with RIM-BP2 in β-cell lines is ~170 kDa (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: The manuscript presents gel electrophoresis data showing myosin-VIIa at ~170 kDa in β-cell lines.

claim: Myosin-VIIa was identified with RIM-BP2 from exophlin-8-interacting, 150 ~ 190 kDa protein bands in MIN6 cells by LC-MS/MS.
source: As described in Figure 3A, myosin-VIIa was identified with RIM-BP2 from exophlin-8-interacting, 150 ~ 190 kDa protein bands in MIN6 cells by LC-MS/MS.
evidence: The manuscript presents LC-MS/MS data identifying myosin-VIIa in the 150-190 kDa range.

claim: In INS-1 832–13 cells, both minor 260 kDa and major 170 kDa protein bands were similarly downregulated by myosin-VIIa siRNA treatment.
source: Furthermore, in INS-1 832–13 cells, both minor 260 kDa and major 170 kDa protein bands were similarly downregulated by myosin-VIIa siRNA treatment (Figure 9C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblotting data showing downregulation of both 260 kDa and 170 kDa bands by myosin-VIIa siRNA.

claim: Only the 170 kDa protein was pulled down with RIM-BP2 in INS1 832/13 cells expressing OST-tagged RIM-BP2.
source: We found that only the 170 kDa protein was pulled down with RIM-BP2, although the 260 kDa protein was also pulled down after exogenous expression of myosin-VIIa (Figure 9D).
evidence: The manuscript presents pull-down data showing only the 170 kDa form of myosin-VIIa binding to RIM-BP2 endogenously.

claim: The 170 kDa protein is derived from myosin-VIIa endogenously expressed in β-cells.
source: These findings indicate that the 170 kDa protein is derived from myosin-VIIa endogenously expressed in β-cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only the 170 kDa form binds RIM-BP2 endogenously, while the 260 kDa form only appears with exogenous expression.

claim: The 260 kDa protein is derived from transfected myosin-VIIa cDNA and interacts with RIM-BP2 through exophilin-8.
source: By contrast, the 260 kDa protein is derived from transfected myosin-VIIa cDNA and interacts with RIM-BP2 through exophilin-8, because it can directly interact with exophilin-8 but not with RIM-BP2 (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from the pull-down experiments showing that the 260 kDa form binds exophilin-8 directly but requires exophilin-8 to bind RIM-BP2.

claim: Exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2 exhibited similarly wide distributions in fractions 3–10 in sucrose density gradient centrifugation.
source: Exophilin-8 (130 kDa) and RIM-BP2 (150 kDa) exhibited similarly wide distributions in fractions 3–10, whereas both endogenous 170 kDa and 260 kDa myosin-VIIa showed relatively narrower distributions around fractions 6–10.
evidence: The manuscript presents sucrose density gradient centrifugation data showing the distribution of exophilin-8 and RIM-BP2.

claim: Both endogenous 170 kDa and 260 kDa myosin-VIIa showed relatively narrower distributions around fractions 6–10 in sucrose density gradient centrifugation.
source: Exophilin-8 (130 kDa) and RIM-BP2 (150 kDa) exhibited similarly wide distributions in fractions 3–10, whereas both endogenous 170 kDa and 260 kDa myosin-VIIa showed relatively narrower distributions around fractions 6–10.
evidence: The manuscript presents sucrose density gradient centrifugation data showing the distribution of myosin-VIIa.

claim: The sucrose density gradient centrifugation findings are consistent with the ternary complex formation among exophilin-8, RIM-BP2, and myosin-VIIa in the cells.
source: Judged from the positions of molecular mass markers, these findings are consistent with the ternary complex formation among these proteins in the cells, although each protein also appeared to exist as a monomer.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlapping distributions of the proteins in the gradient fractions.

claim: Each protein (exophilin-8, RIM-BP2, myosin-VIIa) also appeared to exist as a monomer.
source: Judged from the positions of molecular mass markers, these findings are consistent with the ternary complex formation among these proteins in the cells, although each protein also appeared to exist as a monomer.
evidence: This is inferred from the wide distribution of proteins across multiple fractions in the sucrose density gradient.

claim: Endogenous myosin-Va and -VIIa and their respective C-terminal tails expressed exogenously in INS-1 832/13 cells were all associated with insulin granules, including those accumulated in the actin-rich cell periphery.
source: Endogenous myosin-Va and -VIIa and their respective C-terminal tails expressed exogenously in INS-1 832/13 cells were all associated with insulin granules, including those accumulated in the actin-rich cell periphery (Figure 10D, Figure 10—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing colocalization of myosin-Va and -VIIa with insulin granules.

claim: Silencing of either myosin-Va or -VIIa decreased insulin secretion.
source: Although silencing of either myosin-Va or -VIIa decreased insulin secretion, only the latter affected the peripheral accumulation of granules (Figure 10A–C, Figure 10—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the two motor proteins may have differential effects on secretory granule positioning.
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing decreased secretion with myosin-Va or -VIIa knockdown.

claim: Only silencing of myosin-VIIa affected the peripheral accumulation of granules.
source: Although silencing of either myosin-Va or -VIIa decreased insulin secretion, only the latter affected the peripheral accumulation of granules (Figure 10A–C, Figure 10—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the two motor proteins may have differential effects on secretory granule positioning.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing disrupted granule localization only with myosin-VIIa knockdown.

claim: The two motor proteins (myosin-Va and -VIIa) may have differential effects on secretory granule positioning.
source: Although silencing of either myosin-Va or -VIIa decreased insulin secretion, only the latter affected the peripheral accumulation of granules (Figure 10A–C, Figure 10—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the two motor proteins may have differential effects on secretory granule positioning.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of myosin-Va and -VIIa knockdown on granule localization.

claim: In pancreatic β-cells, the two isoforms of RIM, RIM1 and RIM2, are expressed.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, the two isoforms of RIM, RIM1 and RIM2, are expressed (Iezzi et al., 2000; Yasuda et al., 2010), and homozygous ablation of RIM2 or RIM-interacting Munc13-1 has been shown to affect insulin secretion profoundly (Kang et al., 2006; Yasuda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iezzi et al., 2000; Yasuda et al., 2010.

claim: Homozygous ablation of RIM2 or RIM-interacting Munc13-1 has been shown to affect insulin secretion profoundly.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, the two isoforms of RIM, RIM1 and RIM2, are expressed (Iezzi et al., 2000; Yasuda et al., 2010), and homozygous ablation of RIM2 or RIM-interacting Munc13-1 has been shown to affect insulin secretion profoundly (Kang et al., 2006; Yasuda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kang et al., 2006; Yasuda et al., 2010.

claim: The L-type Cav1.3 subtype is a predominant VDCC mediating stimulus-induced Ca2+ influx to trigger insulin secretion.
source: The L-type Cav1.3 subtype is a predominant VDCC mediating stimulus-induced Ca2+ influx to trigger insulin secretion (Yang and Berggren, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang and Berggren, 2006.

claim: When RIM1, RIM2, or Cav1.3 were downregulated separately by specific siRNA, glucose-induced insulin secretion was markedly decreased.
source: Consistently, when these proteins were downregulated separately by specific siRNA (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), glucose-induced insulin secretion was markedly decreased (Figure 10A).
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing decreased secretion with RIM1, RIM2, or Cav1.3 knockdown.

claim: The peripheral accumulation of granules was not affected by downregulation of RIM1, RIM2, or Cav1.3.
source: However, the peripheral accumulation of granules was not affected (Figure 10B,C, Figure 10—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these proteins function after granules are recruited to the cell periphery.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing no change in granule localization with RIM1, RIM2, or Cav1.3 knockdown.

claim: RIM1, RIM2, and Cav1.3 function after granules are recruited to the cell periphery.
source: However, the peripheral accumulation of granules was not affected (Figure 10B,C, Figure 10—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these proteins function after granules are recruited to the cell periphery.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockdown of these proteins does not affect granule localization but does affect secretion.

claim: Mice deficient in exophilin-8 exhibit glucose intolerance and impaired insulin secretion in vivo.
source: In the present study, we showed that mice deficient in the Rab27a effector, exophilin-8, exhibit glucose intolerance and impaired insulin secretion in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from glucose tolerance tests and insulin secretion assays in knockout mice.

claim: A new multiprotein complex was identified in which exophilin-8 directly interacts with RIM-BP2 and then binds the actin-motor protein, myosin-VIIa, and the exocytic machinery, such as Cav1.3 and RIM.
source: We further identified a new multiprotein complex, in which exophilin-8 directly interacts with RIM-BP2 and then binds the actin-motor protein, myosin-VIIa, and the exocytic machinery, such as Cav1.3 and RIM.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation and pull-down data showing these interactions.

claim: Disruption of the interaction by ablation or mutation of either exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 leads to loss of polarized granule distribution and to a marked decrease in granule exocytosis.
source: Disruption of the interaction by ablation or mutation of either exophilin-8 or RIM-BP2 leads to loss of polarized granule distribution and to a marked decrease in granule exocytosis.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from knockout mice, knockdown experiments, and mutant rescue experiments showing these effects.

claim: RIM-BP2 also has binding activities to the α1 subunits of L-, N-, and P/Q type VDCC.
source: RIM-BP2 also has binding activities to the α1 subunits of L-, N-, and P/Q type VDCC (Hibino et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hibino et al., 2002.

claim: RIM, originally identified as an effector of Rab3, binds and activates a priming factor, Munc13-1.
source: On the other hand, RIM, originally identified as an effector of Rab3 (Wang et al., 1997), binds and activates a priming factor, Munc13-1 (Deng et al., 2011), and also has binding activities to N- and P/Q type VDCC, but not to L-type VDCC (Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 1997; Deng et al., 2011.

claim: RIM has binding activities to N- and P/Q type VDCC, but not to L-type VDCC.
source: On the other hand, RIM, originally identified as an effector of Rab3 (Wang et al., 1997), binds and activates a priming factor, Munc13-1 (Deng et al., 2011), and also has binding activities to N- and P/Q type VDCC, but not to L-type VDCC (Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaeser et al., 2011.

claim: RIM binds Rab3, but not Rab27.
source: Because RIM binds Rab3, but not Rab27 (Fukuda, 2003), and because exophilin-8 binds Rab27, but not Rab3 (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002), the RIM-BP2–myosin-VIIa complex can theoretically associate with granules via either Rab27a–exophilin-8 or Rab3–RIM (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fukuda, 2003.

claim: Exophilin-8 binds Rab27, but not Rab3.
source: Because RIM binds Rab3, but not Rab27 (Fukuda, 2003), and because exophilin-8 binds Rab27, but not Rab3 (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002), the RIM-BP2–myosin-VIIa complex can theoretically associate with granules via either Rab27a–exophilin-8 or Rab3–RIM (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002.

claim: The RIM-BP2–myosin-VIIa complex can theoretically associate with granules via either Rab27a–exophilin-8 or Rab3–RIM.
source: Because RIM binds Rab3, but not Rab27 (Fukuda, 2003), and because exophilin-8 binds Rab27, but not Rab3 (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002), the RIM-BP2–myosin-VIIa complex can theoretically associate with granules via either Rab27a–exophilin-8 or Rab3–RIM (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is inferred from the known binding specificities of RIM and exophilin-8 for different Rab proteins.

claim: An interaction of exophilin-8 with myosin-Va has been shown in heterologous cells and in vitro.
source: Although an interaction of exophilin-8 with myosin-Va has been shown in heterologous cells and in vitro (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002; Desnos et al., 2003), we cannot find evidence that the two proteins act together in secretory cells: they do not form a complex and silencing of myosin-Va does not affect peripheral granule accumulation unlike that of exophilin-8, although it is possible that the degree of myosin-Va depletion in our experimental condition is enough to decrease insulin secretion, but not to affect granule localization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002; Desnos et al., 2003.

claim: Exophilin-8 and myosin-Va do not form a complex in secretory cells.
source: Although an interaction of exophilin-8 with myosin-Va has been shown in heterologous cells and in vitro (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002; Desnos et al., 2003), we cannot find evidence that the two proteins act together in secretory cells: they do not form a complex and silencing of myosin-Va does not affect peripheral granule accumulation unlike that of exophilin-8, although it is possible that the degree of myosin-Va depletion in our experimental condition is enough to decrease insulin secretion, but not to affect granule localization.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing no interaction between exophilin-8 and myosin-Va in secretory cells.

claim: Silencing of myosin-Va does not affect peripheral granule accumulation unlike that of exophilin-8.
source: Although an interaction of exophilin-8 with myosin-Va has been shown in heterologous cells and in vitro (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002; Desnos et al., 2003), we cannot find evidence that the two proteins act together in secretory cells: they do not form a complex and silencing of myosin-Va does not affect peripheral granule accumulation unlike that of exophilin-8, although it is possible that the degree of myosin-Va depletion in our experimental condition is enough to decrease insulin secretion, but not to affect granule localization.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing no change in granule localization with myosin-Va knockdown.

claim: It is possible that the degree of myosin-Va depletion in the experimental condition is enough to decrease insulin secretion, but not to affect granule localization.
source: Although an interaction of exophilin-8 with myosin-Va has been shown in heterologous cells and in vitro (Fukuda and Kuroda, 2002; Desnos et al., 2003), we cannot find evidence that the two proteins act together in secretory cells: they do not form a complex and silencing of myosin-Va does not affect peripheral granule accumulation unlike that of exophilin-8, although it is possible that the degree of myosin-Va depletion in our experimental condition is enough to decrease insulin secretion, but not to affect granule localization.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Exophilin-8 does not interact with myosin-Va under physiological conditions in MIN6 cells, where only the brain-isoform of myosin-Va is expressed.
source: For example, exophilin-8 does not interact with myosin-Va under physiological conditions in MIN6 cells, where only the brain-isoform of myosin-Va is expressed (Brozzi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brozzi et al., 2012.

claim: Exophilin-8 and myosin-Va show negligible physical and functional interactions in the melanocyte cell line, Melan-a, where the melanocyte-isoform of myosin-Va is expressed.
source: Furthermore, these two proteins show negligible physical and functional interactions in the melanocyte cell line, Melan-a, where the melanocyte-isoform of myosin-Va is expressed (Kuroda and Fukuda, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuroda and Fukuda, 2005.

claim: Myosin-VIIa associates with secretory granules and indirectly interacts with exophilin-8 via RIM-BP2.
source: We instead show that myosin-VIIa associates with secretory granules and indirectly interacts with exophilin-8 via RIM-BP2.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining and immunoprecipitation data showing these associations and interactions.

claim: Silencing of myosin-VIIa disrupts granule clustering in the actin-rich cell periphery and markedly decreases stimulus-induced granule exocytosis.
source: Furthermore, silencing of myosin-VIIa disrupts granule clustering in the actin-rich cell periphery and markedly decreases stimulus-induced granule exocytosis, as does the silencing of exophilin-8.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining and insulin secretion assay data showing these effects of myosin-VIIa knockdown.

claim: Myosin-VIIa appears to function in the anchoring, rather than in the active transport, of granules within the F-actin network.
source: Myosin-VIIa appears to function in the anchoring, rather than in the active transport, of granules within the F-actin network, because exophilin-8-positive granules are markedly immobile in the resting state in living cells (Desnos et al., 2003; Mizuno et al., 2011; Huet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from previous observations of granule immobility and supported by citations.

claim: Exophilin-8-positive granules are markedly immobile in the resting state in living cells.
source: Myosin-VIIa appears to function in the anchoring, rather than in the active transport, of granules within the F-actin network, because exophilin-8-positive granules are markedly immobile in the resting state in living cells (Desnos et al., 2003; Mizuno et al., 2011; Huet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desnos et al., 2003; Mizuno et al., 2011; Huet et al., 2012.

claim: The 170 kDa form of myosin-VIIa may represent an alternatively spliced form that specifically functions in secretory cells.
source: Because this form does not appear to be generated from transfected myosin-VIIa cDNA in INS1 832/13 cells, it may represent an alternatively spliced form that specifically functions in secretory cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the 170 kDa form is only seen endogenously and not from transfected cDNA.

claim: Such a small myosin-VIIa isoform has been reported in the UCSC Genome Browser.
source: In fact, such a small myosin-VIIa isoform has been reported in the UCSC Genome Browser (https://genome.ucsc.edu/).
evidence: This is stated as information from a genomic database.

claim: Among the four alternatively spliced isoforms of myosin-VIa, the small insert isoform specifically tethers secretory granules to the cortical actin.
source: It has recently been shown that, among the four alternatively spliced isoforms of the minus-ended motor, myosin-VIa, the small insert isoform specifically tethers secretory granules to the cortical actin (Tomatis et al., 2013), although its molecular link to granules, such as Rab and its effector, has not been identified.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tomatis et al., 2013.

claim: The molecular link of the small insert isoform of myosin-VIa to granules, such as Rab and its effector, has not been identified.
source: It has recently been shown that, among the four alternatively spliced isoforms of the minus-ended motor, myosin-VIa, the small insert isoform specifically tethers secretory granules to the cortical actin (Tomatis et al., 2013), although its molecular link to granules, such as Rab and its effector, has not been identified.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The exophilin-8–RIM-BP2–170 kDa–myosin-VIIa complex formation is functionally critical for granule exocytosis.
source: Although the exact molecular nature of the 170 kDa form of myosin-VIIa and its interaction mode with RIM-BP2 are unknown, our findings that either the PA (ABD) exophilin-8 or the ΔSH3 RIM-BP2 fails to restore the peripheral granule accumulation or to rescue the decreased insulin secretion in knockdown or knockout cells strongly indicate that the exophilin-8–RIM-BP2–170 kDa–myosin-VIIa complex formation is functionally critical for granule exocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that mutants unable to form the complex fail to restore function.

claim: Roles for myosin-VIIa are well-documented in actin-rich protrusion, such as stereocilia of cochlear and vestibular hair cells and microvilli in intestine brush borders and photoreceptor cells.
source: Currently, roles for myosin-VIIa are well-documented in actin-rich protrusion, such as stereocilia of cochlear and vestibular hair cells and microvilli in intestine brush borders and photoreceptor cells (Yan and Liu, 2010; Lu et al., 2014), but no such roles have been identified in granule anchoring or trafficking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yan and Liu, 2010; Lu et al., 2014.

claim: No roles for myosin-VIIa have been identified in granule anchoring or trafficking prior to this study.
source: Currently, roles for myosin-VIIa are well-documented in actin-rich protrusion, such as stereocilia of cochlear and vestibular hair cells and microvilli in intestine brush borders and photoreceptor cells (Yan and Liu, 2010; Lu et al., 2014), but no such roles have been identified in granule anchoring or trafficking.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: There may be parallel secretory pathways bypassing the exophilin-8–RIM-BP2–myosin-VIIa complex formation.
source: This may be because of the existence of parallel secretory pathways bypassing the complex formation: all the granules may not be captured within the cortical F-actin network, or some granules may be captured there by other mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation to explain why exophilin-8-null islets retain some insulin secretion.

claim: All the granules may not be captured within the cortical F-actin network.
source: This may be because of the existence of parallel secretory pathways bypassing the complex formation: all the granules may not be captured within the cortical F-actin network, or some granules may be captured there by other mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation to explain the partial phenotype in knockout cells.

claim: Some granules may be captured within the cortical F-actin network by other mechanisms.
source: This may be because of the existence of parallel secretory pathways bypassing the complex formation: all the granules may not be captured within the cortical F-actin network, or some granules may be captured there by other mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation to explain the partial phenotype in knockout cells.

claim: Exophilin-8-null islets preserve approximately half of the normal level insulin secretion in response to glucose or depolarization stimulation.
source: In fact, exophilin-8-null islets preserve approximately half of the normal level insulin secretion in response to glucose or depolarization stimulation.
evidence: The manuscript presents insulin secretion assay data showing partial preservation of secretion in knockout islets.

claim: Exophilin-8-null pancreatic β-cells exhibit a decrease in the number of granules close to the plasma membrane under electron microscopy.
source: Under electron microscopy, exophilin-8-null pancreatic β-cells exhibit a decrease in the number of granules close to the plasma membrane, but still harbor docked granules whose limiting membrane is directly attached to the membrane.
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data showing reduced granule numbers near the plasma membrane.

claim: Exophilin-8-null pancreatic β-cells still harbor docked granules whose limiting membrane is directly attached to the membrane.
source: Under electron microscopy, exophilin-8-null pancreatic β-cells exhibit a decrease in the number of granules close to the plasma membrane, but still harbor docked granules whose limiting membrane is directly attached to the membrane.
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data showing docked granules in knockout cells.

claim: β-cells deficient in granuphilin exhibit a much greater decrease in the number of granules close to the plasma membrane compared to exophilin-8-null cells.
source: Using the same experimental protocol, we previously demonstrated that β-cells deficient in another Rab27 effector, granuphilin, exhibit a much greater decrease in the number of granules close to the plasma membrane, and almost complete loss of docked granules (Gomi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gomi et al., 2005.

claim: β-cells deficient in granuphilin exhibit almost complete loss of docked granules.
source: Using the same experimental protocol, we previously demonstrated that β-cells deficient in another Rab27 effector, granuphilin, exhibit a much greater decrease in the number of granules close to the plasma membrane, and almost complete loss of docked granules (Gomi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gomi et al., 2005.

claim: The granule number decrease in granuphilin-null β-cells occurs in a more restricted area, with granule centers residing within 200 nm of the plasma membrane.
source: It is notable that the granule number decrease in granuphilin-null β-cells occurs in a more restricted area, with granule centers residing within 200 nm of the plasma membrane, whereas the centers in exophilin-8-null β-cells are within 300 nm.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the electron microscopy data from granuphilin-null and exophilin-8-null cells.

claim: The granule number decrease in exophilin-8-null β-cells occurs with granule centers within 300 nm of the plasma membrane.
source: It is notable that the granule number decrease in granuphilin-null β-cells occurs in a more restricted area, with granule centers residing within 200 nm of the plasma membrane, whereas the centers in exophilin-8-null β-cells are within 300 nm.
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data showing this distribution in exophilin-8-null cells.

claim: The difference in the distance of granule centers from the plasma membrane between granuphilin-null and exophilin-8-null cells has a significant effect on the number of the granules directly attached to the plasma membrane.
